title: What If You Fell Through the Earth? The Full 38-Minute Trip
thought_experiment: Labelled thought experiment: a straight, sealed, airless tunnel; no heat, no Earth rotation. 'Perfect planet' means a uniform-density Earth; 'real Earth' means the PREM density model used by Klotz (2015).
pick_reason: Weekly long video expands one Short from the last seven days. Per-Short views were not re-read (vidiq_user_videos costs 5 credits). earth-tunnel was chosen as the topic with the most to add, and because What If is the channel's best-holding series (PLAYBOOK 2e).

chapters.title: Does gravity get stronger as you fall?
The ride: weightless at orbital speed
Why London to Paris takes longer
The secret: your fall is an orbit

parts.text: You just fell into a hole through Earth.
Where do you stop?
The tunnel is sealed and empty, and the far side is thirty-eight minutes away.
On a perfect, even planet, the same fall takes forty-two.
parts.tts: On a perfect, even planet, the same fall takes, forty-two.

parts.text: So why does the real Earth get you there four minutes sooner?
By the end, you'll see why this fall keeps perfect time with a satellite,
and why a short tunnel from London to Paris would take longer than the whole planet.
First question.
As you fall, does gravity get stronger, or weaker?
Only the Earth below you pulls you down.
The rock above you pulls in every direction at once, so its pull cancels out.
On a perfect, even planet, that means gravity fades steadily,
all the way down to zero at the centre.
But the real Earth isn't even.
Its core is mostly iron, packed far tighter than the rock above it.
So as you drop through the mantle, you leave very little mass behind you,
while you close in on that heavy core.
Gravity actually gets stronger.
It peaks at the edge of the core, about a tenth stronger than at the surface,
and only then falls to zero.
That extra pull is the first clue to our missing four minutes.
So what does the ride actually feel like?
From the moment you drop, you're weightless, like an astronaut,
because you and everything around you are falling together.
The pull gets gentler near the middle, but it never lets go,
so you keep gaining speed, all the way to the centre.
There, gravity is zero, and on a perfect planet you're moving at about eight kilometres every second.
That's fast enough to orbit the Earth.
Nothing pushes back, so you shoot straight through.
Now every metre is uphill. You slow, and slow,
parts.tts: Now every metre is uphill. You slow... and slow,

parts.text: and reach the far side just as your speed hits zero.
On the real Earth, that strong pull deep down gets you moving faster, sooner.
That's where the four minutes went.
Your perfect-planet twin is still climbing,
four minutes behind, toward a finish line you've already crossed.
But here's the strange part.
The tunnel doesn't have to go through the middle.
Dig it at a slant, from London to Paris.
Now gravity points partly into the wall, and only a slice of it pulls you along.
But the tunnel is also far shorter.
And on a perfect planet, those two effects cancel exactly.
A short hop, a long one, or straight through the centre:
every straight tunnel takes the same forty-two minutes.
Even a tunnel a few kilometres long, under a single city,
would still take forty-two minutes.
On the real Earth, short tunnels stay near forty-two, while the longest drop toward thirty-eight.
So London to Paris would take longer than falling through the whole planet.
Why? A short tunnel never leaves the outer rock,
so it never feels that extra pull near the core.
Only the long ones dive deep enough to use it.
So why hasn't anyone built one?
Start with air.
Drag steals a little speed on every swing,
so you rock back and forth, less each time, until you hang at the centre.
Then there's heat.
Near the centre, the Earth is about six thousand degrees Celsius, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
The outer core is liquid metal,
and the pressure down there is millions of times the air pressure on your skin.
No wall we know how to build would hold.
And the deepest hole ever drilled, in northern Russia, stopped about twelve kilometres down.
That's not even a fifth of one percent of the way to the centre.
The rock at the bottom was already as hot as an oven.
So this stays a thought experiment.
But it hides one last surprise.
Remember that top speed? Fast enough to orbit.
Picture a satellite skimming just above the ground, with no air to slow it,
passing overhead at the moment you jump.
On a perfect planet, one lap takes eighty-four minutes.
Half a lap is forty-two.
Seen from the side, the satellite's pull toward the middle grows with its distance from the centre,
just like yours does in the tunnel.
Now watch its shadow on the tunnel.
It moves exactly like you.
Same top speed at the centre, same arrival at the far side.
Your fall is an orbit, seen edge on.
Turn the circle sideways, and the satellite simply becomes you.
And every straight tunnel swings to the beat of that same orbit.
So where do you stop?
In an empty tunnel, you don't.
You fall, and rise, and fall again, keeping time with a satellite you'll never see.

sources: Fall time through a straight tunnel via the centre: 38 min 11 s with the PREM density model, 42 min 12 s for a uniform-density Earth (38 min 0 s with constant gravity). Klotz, A. R. (2015), 'The gravity tunnel in a non-uniform Earth', American Journal of Physics 83, 231, doi:10.1119/1.4898780; arXiv:1308.1342. The four-minute gap is 42:12 minus 38:11.
Only the mass below you pulls (the outer shell's pull cancels): Newton's shell theorem, as used in Klotz 2015 Sec. II.

Uniform Earth: gravity falls linearly to zero at the centre. Real Earth: 'the gravitational field strength actually increases below the surface, reaching a maximum of about 1.09 g, before decreasing in a roughly linear matter through the core to the center', with density reaching 13 tonnes per cubic metre at the centre (Klotz 2015, PREM).
Core is mostly iron, denser than the mantle; core-mantle boundary about 2,900 km deep: USGS, 'This Dynamic Earth: Inside the Earth' (pubs.usgs.gov/gip/dynamic/inside.html).
Weightless during the fall: free fall, no contact with the walls in a frictionless airless tunnel (standard mechanics; the traveller and capsule share the same acceleration).

Peak speed at the centre near 8 km/s for a uniform Earth, and the period and peak speed 'are the same for a circular orbit at Earth's surface'; oscillation period 84 minutes, so 42 minutes to fall through (Klotz 2015 Sec. II.1). Shown as a speed bar; the PREM peak speed is not quoted in the video.

Arrival at the far side with zero speed and endless oscillation without friction: energy conservation in the same model (Klotz 2015; standard gravity-train result). With air, drag damps the swing until the traveller rests at the centre (phys.org, 2015-03, 'New way to calculate how long it would take to fall through a hole in the Earth', notes the textbook answer ignores air resistance).

Any chord takes the same time in a uniform Earth: 'any cord path ... can be traversed in the same amount of time' (Klotz 2015; Cooper, P. W. (1966) 'Through the Earth in forty minutes', Am. J. Phys. 34, 68). Real Earth: 'the PREM time decreases with increasing path length, from near 42 minutes for short paths ... to 38 minutes as it approaches the diameter-length fall' (Klotz 2015). London to Paris is a short chord, so near 42 minutes, longer than the 38-minute diameter fall.

Temperature near the centre about 6,000 C (6000 +/- 500 C at the inner core boundary): ESRF press release, 25 April 2013, on Anzellini et al. (2013), Science 340, 464. Sun's visible surface about 5,500 C: NASA, science.nasa.gov/sun/facts.

Outer core is liquid metal (iron-nickel): National Geographic Education, 'Core' (education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/core); USGS 'Inside the Earth'. Pressure 'millions of times' air pressure: PREM gives about 136 GPa at the core-mantle boundary and about 364 GPa at the centre (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25, 297), i.e. roughly 1.3 to 3.6 million atmospheres.

Satellite's sideways pull grows with its sideways distance: for a circular orbit at the surface, the component of gravity along the tunnel is g times x over R, the same law as inside a uniform Earth (Klotz 2015: period and peak speed are the same as for a circular orbit at Earth's surface).
Short tunnels stay near 42 minutes in the real Earth because they stay in the outer layers; long ones pass through the strong-gravity region near the core (Klotz 2015, Sec. III, chord paths in PREM).

Deepest hole: Kola Superdeep Borehole, about 12,262 m, drilling stopped 1992, bottom temperature about 180 C ('almost twice as hot as they'd predicted'): Scientific American, 'How deep is the deepest hole in the world?'. 12.262 km / 6,371 km mean radius = 0.19%, i.e. under a fifth of one percent. 'As hot as an oven' refers to 180 C, a typical home baking temperature.

Simplifications, labelled on screen: thought experiment; no heat, no air (except where shown), no Earth rotation; the satellite-shadow picture is exact only for the uniform 'perfect planet' (Klotz 2015).
